title: Mouth, teeth and pharynx
summary: Where digestion starts: chewing, saliva and swallowing.

layers.basics: Teeth grind food and saliva begins breaking down starch. Your tongue pushes the food to the throat to swallow.
layers.deeper: Salivary glands release about 1-1.5 L of saliva daily containing amylase and lipase. Swallowing is a reflex coordinated by the brainstem.
layers.expert: Swallowing has oral, pharyngeal and esophageal phases; the epiglottis diverts food from the airway; adults have 32 teeth, and enamel is ≈ 96% mineral (hydroxyapatite).

did_you_know: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.

title: Esophagus
summary: A muscular tube that carries swallowed food to the stomach.

layers.basics: The food pipe pushes your food down by waves of squeezing, so you can even swallow upside down.
layers.deeper: Upper third is skeletal muscle, lower third smooth muscle, with sphincters at both ends.
layers.expert: Peristalsis driven by the vagus and enteric plexuses; lower esophageal sphincter prevents reflux; stratified squamous epithelium.

did_you_know: Astronauts can swallow in zero gravity because muscles, not gravity, move food.

title: Stomach
summary: A stretchy muscular sac that churns food with acid and enzymes.

layers.basics: The stomach mixes food into a thick soup called chyme and starts breaking down protein.
layers.deeper: It can hold about 1-1.5 L; gastric juice has a pH around 1.5-3.5, strong enough to kill most microbes.
layers.expert: Parietal cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factor, chief cells release pepsinogen, G cells secrete gastrin; mucus-bicarbonate layer protects the wall; emptying ≈ 2-4 h.

did_you_know: The stomach lining is shielded from its own acid by a thick layer of bicarbonate-rich mucus and by tight junctions between its cells, and the surface cells are also replaced every 3 to 6 days.

title: Gastric pits and glands
summary: Tiny pits in the stomach lining that release acid, enzymes and mucus.

layers.basics: The stomach wall is dotted with millions of little pits that pour out digestive juices.
layers.deeper: Different cells in each gland make acid, enzymes, mucus and hormones.
layers.expert: Parietal cells (H+/K+ ATPase), chief cells (pepsinogen), mucous neck cells, enteroendocrine G cells; stem cells at the isthmus.

did_you_know: Parietal cell proton pumps push acid into the stomach against a gradient of many thousand-fold or more in H+ concentration, because the cell interior stays near neutral pH.

title: Small intestine
summary: A long coiled tube where most digestion and absorption of nutrients happen.

layers.basics: This is where most food becomes usable nutrients, absorbed through a huge folded lining.
layers.deeper: It has three parts: duodenum, jejunum and ileum. Bile and pancreatic enzymes enter the duodenum.
layers.expert: Circular folds, villi and microvilli multiply the surface; modern measurements give villi plus microvilli about 60-120-fold and about 30 m² for the small intestine (older texts quote 200-300 m²); brush border enzymes finish digestion; segmentation and migrating motor complexes mix and move contents.

did_you_know: Despite the name 'small', it is the longest part of your digestive tube.

title: Intestinal villi
summary: Finger-like projections that greatly increase the intestine's absorption area.

layers.basics: Villi are tiny fingers covering the inner wall, soaking up nutrients.
layers.deeper: Each villus has capillaries for sugars and amino acids and a lymph vessel (lacteal) for fats.
layers.expert: Enterocytes carry microvilli (brush border) ≈ 1 µm tall; crypts of Lieberkühn house stem cells; epithelial turnover ≈ 3-5 days.

did_you_know: The intestinal lining is replaced every 3 to 5 days, one of the fastest turnover rates in the body.

title: Large intestine (colon)
summary: The wide tube that absorbs water and salts and houses most gut microbes.

layers.basics: The large intestine turns leftovers into stool and hosts trillions of helpful bacteria.
layers.deeper: It includes cecum, colon and rectum. Gut microbes ferment fiber into useful fatty acids.
layers.expert: Colonic transit is far slower than the 3-5 hours chyme spends in the small intestine; microbial fermentation gives short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate) used by colonocytes; microbial density in colon contents is very high, on the order of 10^11 bacterial cells per millilitre of content (roughly per gram).

facts: ≈ 1.5-1.7 m (about a third of the ≈ 5 m gut; varies widely)
most of the ≈ 10% that reaches the colon
did_you_know: Bacteria make up a large share of stool, and the share depends on diet.

title: Gut microbiome
summary: The community of trillions of microbes living mainly in the large intestine.

layers.basics: Your gut hosts bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses that help digest fiber, train the immune system and make vitamins.
layers.deeper: Their composition varies between people and over time, shaped by diet, age and environment.
layers.expert: Metagenomic sequencing of 124 Europeans (2010) found at least 160 bacterial species in each person and 1,000-1,150 prevalent species across the whole group; causal links to obesity, mood or disease are actively researched, and many associations remain correlational.

did_you_know: The ratio of microbial to human cells is closer to 1:1 than the older 10:1 estimate.
open_questions: Which microbiome features cause (rather than merely correlate with) health effects?
How reliably can microbiome interventions treat disease?

title: Liver
summary: The largest internal organ, which processes nutrients, makes bile and detoxifies the blood.

layers.basics: The liver is a chemical factory that cleans blood, stores energy and makes bile to digest fats.
layers.deeper: It receives blood both from the gut (portal vein) and from the heart (hepatic artery), and can regrow after partial removal.
layers.expert: Performs a very wide range of functions, including glycogen storage, gluconeogenesis, albumin and clotting-factor synthesis, the urea cycle, cytochrome P450 drug metabolism and bile-acid production.

did_you_know: The liver can regenerate to full size from as little as a quarter of its mass.

title: Liver lobule
summary: Roughly hexagonal units of liver tissue, only faintly outlined in humans, where blood is processed.

layers.basics: Blood flows through each lobule, passing liver cells that clean it.
layers.deeper: Blood flows from the corners (portal triads) toward a central vein.
layers.expert: Sinusoids, Kupffer cells, stellate cells; zonation (periportal to pericentral) specializes metabolism.

did_you_know: Each lobule is only about 1-2 mm across, and in humans its edges are barely visible in ordinary stained sections.

title: Gallbladder
summary: A small sac that stores and concentrates bile.

layers.basics: The gallbladder holds bile until fatty food arrives, then squeezes it into the intestine.
layers.deeper: Bile salts break fat into small droplets so that lipase can reach it; between meals the gallbladder removes water and concentrates bile.
layers.expert: CCK triggers gallbladder contraction and sphincter of Oddi relaxation; bile is concentrated by up to about 10-fold; cholesterol stones are common.

did_you_know: People can live normally without a gallbladder.

title: Pancreas
summary: A gland that makes digestive enzymes and the hormones insulin and glucagon.

layers.basics: The pancreas does two jobs: it sends enzymes to the intestine and hormones to the blood.
layers.deeper: Most of it (acinar tissue) makes enzymes; small clusters of cells called islets make hormones.
layers.expert: Exocrine secretion (≈ 1-1.5 L/day) includes trypsinogen, amylase, lipase and bicarbonate; endocrine islets contain alpha, beta, delta cells.

did_you_know: The name pancreas comes from Greek for 'all flesh'.

title: Pancreatic islets
summary: Clusters of cells in the pancreas that make insulin and glucagon.

layers.basics: About a million tiny islands of cells that monitor your blood sugar.
layers.deeper: Beta cells release insulin to lower blood sugar; alpha cells release glucagon to raise it.
layers.expert: ≈ 1-2% of pancreatic mass; beta cells ≈ 50-70% of islet; glucose sensing via GLUT/glucokinase and K-ATP channels triggers insulin exocytosis.

did_you_know: Islets make up only about 1-2% of the pancreas.

title: Left kidney
summary: The left kidney filters blood and makes urine.

layers.basics: Kidneys are bean-shaped organs that clean your blood and control water, salt and acid levels.
layers.deeper: Each has about a million nephrons. Blood enters via the renal artery, filtered fluid becomes urine collected in the renal pelvis.
layers.expert: Receives ≈ 25% of cardiac output at rest; GFR ≈ 105-125 mL/min; also secretes renin, erythropoietin and activates vitamin D (calcitriol).

did_you_know: Each kidney is only about the size of a fist, but together they receive about a quarter of the blood the heart pumps at rest.

title: Right kidney
summary: The right kidney filters blood and makes urine.

layers.basics: Kidneys are bean-shaped organs that clean your blood and control water, salt and acid levels.
layers.deeper: Each has about a million nephrons. Blood enters via the renal artery, filtered fluid becomes urine collected in the renal pelvis.
layers.expert: Receives ≈ 25% of cardiac output at rest; GFR ≈ 105-125 mL/min; also secretes renin, erythropoietin and activates vitamin D (calcitriol).

did_you_know: Each kidney is only about the size of a fist, but together they receive about a quarter of the blood the heart pumps at rest.

title: Renal cortex
summary: The outer layer of the kidney holding the filters.

layers.basics: The outer shell where blood is first filtered.
layers.deeper: It contains glomeruli and most of the tubules.
layers.expert: Cortical labyrinth and medullary rays; most nephrons are cortical, with a minority lying close to the medulla (juxtamedullary).

facts: all glomeruli, plus the first parts of the tubules
did_you_know: About a fifth of the plasma flowing through the kidney is filtered.

title: Renal medulla
summary: Inner region with cone-shaped pyramids that concentrate urine.

layers.basics: The inner part drains urine and concentrates it.
layers.deeper: Pyramids of collecting ducts and loops of Henle.
layers.expert: Osmotic gradient from ≈ 300 to ≈ 1200 mOsm/kg establishes countercurrent multiplication.

did_you_know: The salt gradient of the medulla rises from about 300 mOsm/kg near the cortex to about 1200 mOsm/kg deep inside, roughly four times the osmolality of blood.

title: Renal pelvis
summary: The funnel where urine collects before flowing to the ureter.

layers.basics: Urine collects here and then flows down the ureter.
layers.deeper: Minor and major calyces feed into it.
layers.expert: Peristalsis of calyces and pelvis propels urine; urothelium resists toxicity of urine.

did_you_know: A kidney stone often gets stuck where the pelvis meets the ureter.

title: Nephron
summary: The kidney's microscopic filtering and processing unit.

layers.basics: Each nephron filters blood and then takes back the water and nutrients your body wants to keep.
layers.deeper: It consists of a glomerulus and a long tubule with several regions; the tubule drains into a collecting duct, which is continuous with the nephron but usually counted as a separate structure.
layers.expert: Segments: Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule (≈ 65% reabsorption), loop of Henle, distal tubule, connecting tubule; juxtaglomerular apparatus regulates GFR via tubuloglomerular feedback.

did_you_know: Each kidney holds more than a million of these filter-and-tube units, all working side by side.

title: Glomerulus
summary: A tuft of capillaries where blood plasma is filtered.

layers.basics: Blood is pushed against a super-fine sieve; water and small molecules pass, cells and big proteins stay.
layers.deeper: Three layers: fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, podocyte slit diaphragms.
layers.expert: Filtration fraction ≈ 20%; filtration pressure ≈ 10 mmHg net; podocytes' nephrin slit-diaphragm restricts albumin.

did_you_know: The kidneys filter about 150-180 L of plasma a day (GFR ≈ 105-125 mL/min) yet make only 1-2 L of urine.

title: Proximal convoluted tubule
summary: The first long tube segment that reclaims most water, salt and all glucose.

layers.basics: Most of what you need (sugar, water, salts) is taken back here.
layers.deeper: Brush border and abundant mitochondria support active transport.
layers.expert: Na+-coupled transport (SGLT2 takes up glucose); ≈ 65% of Na+ and water reabsorbed; secretion of organic acids and bases.

did_you_know: Normally nearly all filtered glucose is reabsorbed here, so none appears in urine.

title: Loop of Henle
summary: A hairpin that builds the salt gradient used to concentrate urine.

layers.basics: The loop of Henle dips into the kidney's inner zone, building a salty gradient so the body can make concentrated urine.
layers.deeper: Descending limb is water-permeable, ascending thick limb pumps out salt (NKCC2).
layers.expert: The thick ascending limb pumps Na+, K+ and Cl- out through the NKCC2 symporter but is nearly impermeable to water, so the surrounding tissue grows saltier; the hairpin shape multiplies this effect (countercurrent multiplication); loop diuretics block NKCC2; vasa recta capillaries preserve the gradient.

did_you_know: Deep in the medulla the filtrate can reach about 1200 mOsmol/kg, roughly four times the osmolality of blood.

title: Distal convoluted tubule
summary: The fine-tuning segment that adjusts salt and calcium.

layers.basics: Hormones adjust the final salt and calcium balance here.
layers.deeper: Aldosterone and PTH act on segments here.
layers.expert: NCC transporter (thiazide target); PTH raises Ca2+ reabsorption here; aldosterone acts mainly on the late distal tubule and the collecting duct; the macula densa, at the start of the distal tubule where it touches the glomerular arterioles, belongs to the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

did_you_know: Thiazide diuretics block the NCC salt transporter in this segment.

title: Collecting duct
summary: The final tube that gathers urine and sets its water content.

layers.basics: The last stop for adjusting urine's water content, controlled by the hormone ADH.
layers.deeper: Water channels (aquaporin-2) are inserted when ADH is high, making urine concentrated.
layers.expert: Principal cells (ENaC, AQP2) and intercalated cells (acid-base); urea recycling in the inner medulla.

did_you_know: With ADH present, water leaves the collecting duct and urine becomes concentrated; without it, urine stays dilute.

title: Ureters
summary: Two muscular tubes carrying urine from the kidneys to the bladder.

layers.basics: Waves of muscle squeeze urine down these thin tubes, even if you're lying down.
layers.deeper: Waves of peristalsis push urine along; the pace depends on how much urine is flowing.
layers.expert: Urothelium; three constrictions (pelviureteric junction, pelvic brim, vesicoureteric junction) are common stone-lodging sites.

facts: a few mm, narrower at its three constrictions
did_you_know: They enter the bladder at an angle, forming a one-way valve.

title: Urinary bladder
summary: A stretchy muscular bag that stores urine.

layers.basics: The bladder fills like a balloon and signals when it's time to go.
layers.deeper: It can hold up to about 500-600 mL; the first urge is sensed at about 150 mL and is easily overridden, and control becomes hard to keep as the volume nears 300-400 mL.
layers.expert: Detrusor smooth muscle and transitional epithelium (urothelium); micturition reflex coordinated by sacral cord (S2-S4) and pontine micturition center; internal and external sphincters.

did_you_know: The bladder wall can stretch to many times its relaxed size without pressure rising much.

title: Urethra
summary: The tube that carries urine out of the body.

layers.basics: The final tube for urine. It is longer in males than in females.
layers.deeper: Sphincters control release.
layers.expert: Female ≈ 4 cm, male ≈ 20 cm; the male urethra also carries semen.

did_you_know: The shorter female urethra, together with its position near the anus, is one reason urinary infections are more common in women.

title: Pituitary gland
summary: A pea-sized gland that controls many other hormone glands.

layers.basics: Called the master gland, it releases hormones controlling growth, stress, thyroid and reproduction.
layers.deeper: The anterior lobe makes hormones like growth hormone and TSH; the posterior lobe releases oxytocin and ADH made in the hypothalamus.
layers.expert: Anterior lobe receives hypophyseal portal blood carrying releasing hormones; posterior is neural tissue releasing OT and AVP.

facts: 8 (6 anterior, 2 released from the posterior lobe)
did_you_know: It sits in a small bony pocket of the skull called the sella turcica.

title: Thyroid
summary: A butterfly-shaped gland in the neck that sets the body's metabolic pace.

layers.basics: The thyroid releases hormones that control how fast your cells use energy.
layers.deeper: It needs iodine to make thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3).
layers.expert: TSH stimulates thyroglobulin iodination; T3 acts via nuclear thyroid hormone receptors; C cells secrete calcitonin.

did_you_know: Iodine-deficiency can cause a swollen thyroid (goiter).

title: Parathyroid glands
summary: Four tiny glands behind the thyroid that control blood calcium.

layers.basics: They monitor calcium in your blood and release a hormone to raise it when low.
layers.deeper: Parathyroid hormone acts on bone, kidney and gut.
layers.expert: PTH release is controlled by the calcium-sensing receptor; PTH increases bone resorption, renal Ca2+ reabsorption and calcitriol synthesis.

did_you_know: Ivar Sandström, a Swedish medical student, first demonstrated them in humans around 1880; the gland had been noticed in a rhinoceros in 1850.

title: Adrenal glands
summary: Two glands atop the kidneys that release stress hormones.

layers.basics: They make adrenaline and cortisol, which help you respond to stress.
layers.deeper: The outer cortex makes steroid hormones; the inner medulla makes adrenaline.
layers.expert: Zones: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens); medulla chromaffin cells secrete epinephrine in response to sympathetic input.

did_you_know: Each adrenal gland weighs about as much as a grape.

title: Pineal gland
summary: A tiny pinecone-shaped gland that releases melatonin in the dark.

layers.basics: It helps tell your body when it's night.
layers.deeper: It is regulated by light signals through the suprachiasmatic nucleus.
layers.expert: Melatonin synthesis from serotonin by AANAT, peaking at night; calcifies with age.

did_you_know: Descartes proposed it as the seat of the soul.

title: Spleen
summary: An organ that filters blood and stores immune cells.

layers.basics: The spleen removes old red blood cells and helps fight infections.
layers.deeper: It has red pulp (filtering) and white pulp (immune cells).
layers.expert: Marginal zone B cells respond to blood-borne encapsulated bacteria; red pulp macrophages recycle iron; the red pulp holds a blood reservoir from which contraction can release some red cells.

did_you_know: A person can live without a spleen but is more vulnerable to some infections.

title: Thymus
summary: Where T cells mature; largest relative to body size in infants and children.

layers.basics: T cells go to school in the thymus, learning to ignore your own body.
layers.deeper: It is most active in childhood and shrinks with age.
layers.expert: Positive and negative selection of thymocytes; thymic involution (shrinkage and fat replacement) is described as beginning after puberty, though T-cell output may start to fall earlier; AIRE expression enables central tolerance.

did_you_know: Mostly fat by old age, yet T cells made earlier persist for decades.

title: Lymph nodes
summary: Bean-shaped filters where immune cells meet germs in the fluid.

layers.basics: Lymph nodes swell when you're sick because defender cells multiply there.
layers.deeper: Lymph drains through them on its way back to the blood.
layers.expert: Afferent lymph enters via the subcapsular sinus; B-cell follicles and T-cell paracortex organize germinal centers.

did_you_know: Swollen glands are usually lymph nodes working.

title: Lymphatic vessels
summary: Thin vessels that collect leaked fluid and return it to the blood.

layers.basics: They drain extra fluid from tissues and carry it back toward the heart.
layers.deeper: Valves keep lymph flowing one way.
layers.expert: Initial lymphatics (lymphatic capillaries) with overlapping endothelial flaps; ≈ 3 L/day returned; thoracic duct drains most of the body.

did_you_know: Lymph is also how dietary fats reach the blood after a meal.

title: Skin
summary: The body's largest organ: a waterproof, sensitive, self-renewing covering.

layers.basics: Skin protects you from germs, UV light and water loss, helps control body temperature and lets you feel.
layers.deeper: Two layers: the epidermis (outer) and the dermis (middle). Beneath them lies the hypodermis, a fatty layer that anchors the skin but is not strictly part of it.
layers.expert: Keratinocyte differentiation produces the stratum corneum; the horny surface layer is replaced about every 4 weeks; melanocytes, Langerhans cells and Merkel cells reside in the epidermis.

facts: varies by site; thickest on palms and soles
did_you_know: Skin is the largest organ of the body by surface area.

title: Epidermis
summary: The thin, outer, waterproof layer of skin.

layers.basics: The outer layer is made of flat dead cells, constantly replaced from below.
layers.deeper: Cells are made at the bottom and move upward, flatten, and fill with keratin.
layers.expert: Five layers in thick skin: basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum; no blood vessels.

did_you_know: The surface layer you see is dead cells.

title: Dermis
summary: The thick middle layer with fibers, vessels and nerves.

layers.basics: It gives skin its strength and stretch.
layers.deeper: Contains collagen, elastin, blood vessels, nerve endings and glands.
layers.expert: Papillary and reticular layers; fibroblasts produce collagen type I and III.

did_you_know: Tattoo ink sits in the dermis, which is why it doesn't wash away.

title: Hair follicle
summary: A pocket in the skin that grows a hair.

layers.basics: Each hair grows from a root in a follicle.
layers.deeper: A hair has a living bulb at the base and a dead keratin shaft.
layers.expert: Growth cycle: anagen, catagen, telogen; dermal papilla signaling; follicles cover most of the body surface, with the densest cover on the scalp.

facts: Hairs lost and replaced per day
did_you_know: On average about 50 hairs are lost and replaced every day.

title: Sweat gland
summary: A coiled tube that releases sweat to cool the body.

layers.basics: Sweat evaporates and cools you down.
layers.deeper: Eccrine glands cover most of the body and are most abundant on the palms, soles and forehead; apocrine glands sit mainly in the armpits and genital region.
layers.expert: Millions of eccrine glands; sweat is mostly water with Na+ and Cl-; cholinergic sympathetic control.

did_you_know: Human skin has by far the highest density of eccrine sweat glands among primates, which is generally linked to cooling by sweat.

title: Hypodermis
summary: The fatty layer under the skin.

layers.basics: It cushions and insulates.
layers.deeper: Made of fat cells and loose tissue.
layers.expert: Fat tissue also acts as an endocrine organ (it releases leptin and adiponectin), and the thickness and distribution of the hypodermis differ by sex and body site.

did_you_know: It anchors the skin to the tissue beneath it while cushioning and insulating the body.

title: Testes
summary: The male gonads, making sperm and testosterone.

layers.basics: Testes produce sperm and the hormone testosterone.
layers.deeper: They hang outside the body where it is slightly cooler.
layers.expert: Spermatogenesis in seminiferous tubules takes ≈ 64-74 days; Leydig cells produce testosterone under LH.

facts: ≈ 10^8 per day (≈ 45-300 million, both testes, healthy adult)
did_you_know: Sperm production works best a few degrees below core body temperature.

title: Ovaries
summary: The female gonads, releasing eggs and hormones.

layers.basics: The ovaries store eggs and make estrogen and progesterone.
layers.deeper: Each cycle, one follicle usually matures and releases an egg.
layers.expert: Follicular development driven by FSH, ovulation triggered by LH surge; ≈ 1-2 million oocytes at birth, ≈ 300-400 ovulated.

did_you_know: Egg cells are present from before birth.

title: Uterus
summary: The muscular organ in which an embryo grows.

layers.basics: The uterus can stretch to hold a growing baby.
layers.deeper: Its inner lining thickens each cycle and is shed if no pregnancy occurs.
layers.expert: Myometrium (smooth muscle) and endometrium; oxytocin drives labor contractions; uterine weight rises from ≈ 70 g to ≈ 1 kg in pregnancy.

did_you_know: During pregnancy the uterus grows many-fold, as its smooth-muscle cells both multiply and enlarge.
